title: The Castle That Made Kings
subtitle: Warwick Castle → Lord Leycester → the Beauchamp Chapel
intro: One castle, one day, and a story that runs from a Norman earth mound in 1068 to a pair of gilt-bronze tombs a ten-minute walk away. Five acts, three live shows, every outdoor stop filmed while the sun is out — and a hard stop at 4 PM.

acts.label: Act 1 · The Norman beginning
acts.tagline: 1068. An earth mound and a decision.
acts.narrative:
Start outside, before you own a ticket. Castle Bridge gives you Caesar's Tower rising straight out of the River Avon with the broken arches of the medieval bridge in the water below, and at twenty past nine the sun is still in the east — the best light you will get all day, for free.

Then go in and climb the Mound first, because that is literally where the story starts. In 1068 William the Conqueror had been king for two years and the Midlands were not settled, so he ordered a motte-and-bailey thrown up at Warwick to hold the road north. The mound under your feet is it. Everything else on this site — every tower, every state room, every gift shop — sits on top of that one decision.

acts.label: Act 2 · The fortress
acts.tagline: Three hundred years later, the Beauchamps build in stone.
acts.narrative:
The trebuchet at 10:45 is your first set-piece and it does a job for you: it makes medieval violence feel slow. Eighteen metres, twenty-two tonnes, a crew of men and several minutes to load one shot. That was a siege — enormous effort, enormous force, very little speed.

Then climb. Caesar's Tower and Guy's Tower went up in the 14th century under Thomas Beauchamp, three hundred years after the Conqueror's earth mound, and they are the reason the castle looks the way it does from the road. Walk the ramparts between them. Film going up the spiral stairs, not coming down.

acts.label: Act 3 · The Kingmaker
acts.tagline: One earl, two kings deposed, dead at 42.
acts.narrative:
This is the centre of the film. Richard Neville, 16th Earl of Warwick, is remembered as Warwick the Kingmaker and he earned the name: he helped put Edward IV on the throne, fell out with him, switched sides and put Henry VI back. Two kings installed, two kings unmade, by one man who was probably richer than the crown he propped up. He was killed at the Battle of Barnet on 14 April 1471 and the family's power died with him.

Tell that story, and then let the 11:45 show illustrate it — it is called Wars of the Roses LIVE, which is about as on-the-nose as an itinerary ever gets. Falconry at 12:30 closes the outdoor half of the day.

acts.label: Act 4 · The long afterlife
acts.narrative:
A castle stays a castle only while somebody needs to defend it. The Grevilles took Warwick in 1604 and spent the next three hundred and seventy years turning a fortress into a house. The Great Hall and State Rooms are that process made visible — and largely a rebuild, because a serious fire gutted part of the range in 1871. This is where the story stops being about war and starts being about money, taste and keeping up appearances.

Then go down to the Mill and Engine House by the river, the least famous thing on site and one of the best: a medieval fortress wired for electric light by Victorian engineers in overalls. It also gives you the strongest low angle on Caesar's Tower anywhere in the grounds.

acts.label: Act 5 · The tombs
acts.tagline: You walked their rooms. Now stand at their graves.
acts.narrative:
Leave the castle at 2:40 and walk into town. The Lord Leycester is a row of crooked timber buildings that began as 14th-century guildhalls; in 1571 Robert Dudley, Earl of Leicester and Elizabeth I's favourite, turned them into a home for broken and retired soldiers. It still is one, 455 years later. They survived the Great Fire of 1694 that flattened the rest of the centre, which is why they look nothing like the Georgian brick around them.

Then the ending. The Beauchamp Chapel at St Mary's was built between 1443 and 1464 to hold Richard Beauchamp, 13th Earl of Warwick, and it took twenty-one years because nobody was willing to do it cheaply. His effigy is gilt bronze. Robert Dudley is in there too — the same man whose almshouse you just walked out of. So you spend a whole day inside the rooms these men built and fought over, and then you stand at their graves. Say that on camera, and stop talking.

kit: Phone or camera — handheld only. Warwick allows personal filming but not commercial rigs; a tripod or gimbal can get you stopped.
Spare battery and a spare card — six and a half hours of filming will kill one battery
AirPods or a clip mic — the arenas are open, loud and windy
Shoes you can climb in: two tower climbs on narrow spiral stairs, plus 163 more if you do the church tower
A light layer — 12°C at 9 AM, 20°C by mid-afternoon
Contactless for parking (£10), Lord Leycester (£9) and the chapel (£5)
preTrip: Book the Warwick Castle standard day ticket online tonight — and do NOT add the Dungeon
Do NOT pre-book Lord Leycester — the 25% castle discount only works at their door
Charge every battery, clear the card
Set phone alarms for 10:40, 11:40 and 12:25 — the three shows are the spine of the day
At the gate, check the show board and confirm 10:45 / 11:45 / 12:30 haven't moved
goldenRule: The three shows are fixed points — 10:45, 11:45, 12:30. Everything else bends around them. Miss one and you lose an act.

castle-bridge.name: Castle Bridge & the River Avon
castle-bridge.angle: The shot that opens the film
castle-bridge.story: Film the cold open here, before you own a ticket. Castle Bridge gives you the classic view: Caesar's Tower rising straight out of the Avon, with the broken arches of the abandoned medieval bridge sitting in the water underneath it. At 9:20 the sun is still in the east and the castle's river front is lit, which makes this the best light of the entire day — and it is free and always open.
facts: There has been a castle on this rock above the Avon since 1068 — 958 years
Caesar's Tower is roughly 44m / 147ft, and has never had anything whatsoever to do with Caesar
The broken arches in the river are the medieval bridge, abandoned when this one opened in 1793
Mill Garden, at the end of Mill Street, has an even better version of this view for a small fee — but it doesn't open until 10:00

routeCard.sub: Castle Bridge, Banbury Road · 9:20 AM · free
routeCard.note: Park first at the Stables car park (CV34 4QU, £10) and walk down — about 5 minutes.

the-mound.name: The Mound
the-mound.story: Climb this first, because the whole story begins here. In 1068 William the Conqueror had been king for two years and the Midlands were still not settled, so he ordered a motte-and-bailey thrown up at Warwick to hold the road north. The motte is the mound you are standing on. Everything else on this site — every tower, every state room, every gift shop — was built on top of that single decision. You also get the layout of the whole castle from the top, which is useful this early in the film.
facts: 1068 — two years after Hastings, with the Conqueror still nailing England down
A motte-and-bailey went up fast: earth mound, timber tower, wooden palisade. Weeks, not years.
Nothing visible from up here is Norman — the stone castle came three hundred years later
Warwick sat on the road north; hold Warwick and you hold the route into the Midlands

trebuchet.name: The Legend of the Trebuchet
trebuchet.angle: Set-piece one — medieval violence, in slow motion
trebuchet.story: The trebuchet on the river bank is one of the largest working siege machines in the world: about eighteen metres, twenty-two tonnes, built from medieval engineering drawings. What makes it good on camera is not the shot, it is the loading — a crew of men, several minutes, enormous effort for one throw. That is what a siege actually was. Two shows a day, 10:45 and 14:00; you want the 10:45 so the afternoon stays free.
facts: Roughly 18m tall and 22 tonnes, built to medieval designs
A trebuchet is a counterweight machine — drop the weight, the arm swings, the shot flies
It takes a crew and several minutes to load one shot. Sieges were slow.
Range is a few hundred metres — enough to break a gate, or lob something unpleasant over a wall

routeCard.sub: River bank, below the castle · 10:45 show
routeCard.note: Included in your day ticket. Get there 5 minutes early for a clear sightline.

planCard.todo: Arrive by 10:40 and stand side-on, not behind — you want the arm's arc across frame. Film the loading, not just the launch.
film: The crew winching — this is the shot people don't get
The launch, wide, arm crossing frame
Reaction piece-to-camera straight after

towers.name: Guy's Tower, Caesar's Tower & the Ramparts
towers.angle: Act two — the Beauchamps build in stone
towers.story: Three hundred years after the Conqueror's earth mound, the Beauchamp earls turned Warwick into serious stone. Thomas Beauchamp raised Caesar's Tower and Guy's Tower in the 14th century and they are the reason the castle still looks like a fortress from the road. Guy's is twelve-sided and about 39 metres; Caesar's is around 44. Climb both and walk the ramparts between them — it is the best elevated footage on the whole site.
facts: Caesar's Tower about 44m/147ft; Guy's Tower about 39m/128ft and twelve-sided
Both 14th century, built under Thomas Beauchamp — the family that made Warwick powerful
Caesar's Tower had a basement dungeon that held French prisoners taken at Poitiers in 1356
Narrow spiral stairs and no lift — the ramparts walk between the towers is the money shot

routeCard.note: Steep, narrow, one-way in places. Not somewhere to be fiddling with a camera bag.

walkPoints.name: Guy's Tower
walkPoints.story: Twelve-sided, about 39 metres, five storeys of guest chambers stacked above each other. Built to impress as much as defend.
walkPoints.todo: Climb it first while your legs are fresh. Film going up — the spiral reads well on camera.

walkPoints.name: The ramparts
walkPoints.story: The curtain wall walk linking the two great towers, looking down into the courtyard on one side and out over the Avon on the other.
walkPoints.todo: Walk it slowly with the camera low and level. Best elevated shot of the day.

walkPoints.name: Caesar's Tower
walkPoints.story: The taller of the two at roughly 44 metres, with a dungeon in the basement that held French knights captured at Poitiers in 1356.
walkPoints.todo: Mention the dungeon and the prisoners — it lands better than the height does.

see: Views over the Avon and the courtyard
planCard.todo: Both towers and the wall between them in thirty minutes. Move — you have to be seated for the jousting at 11:45.

jousting.angle: Act three — the man who made and unmade kings
jousting.story: This is the centre of the film, and the show is your illustration for it. Richard Neville, 16th Earl of Warwick, is remembered as Warwick the Kingmaker: he helped put Edward IV on the throne, fell out with him, switched sides and put Henry VI back. Two kings installed, two kings unmade, by one earl who was probably richer than the crown he propped up. He was killed at the Battle of Barnet on 14 April 1471 and the family's power died with him. Tell that first, then let the horses do the rest.
facts: Richard Neville, 16th Earl of Warwick — 'the Kingmaker' — deposed two kings and installed two
At his peak he was probably wealthier and more powerful than the king he served
Killed at the Battle of Barnet, 14 April 1471, aged about 42
The Wars of the Roses ran 1455–1487 — York against Lancaster, white rose against red
The show runs in a purpose-built River Arena against the castle's south front

falconry.name: The Falconer's Quest
falconry.story: The UK's largest bird of prey display, up to sixty species, flown in an arena over the Avon. It is not strictly part of the castle's story, but hunting with birds is what earls actually did with their afternoons for five hundred years, so it is not a bolt-on either. Visually it is the best moving footage you will get all day. Shows at 12:30 and 16:30 — take the 12:30, because 16:30 is past your stop.
facts: Up to 60 species flown over the river — the largest display of its kind in the UK
Falconry was ranked: the bird you were permitted to fly was fixed by your social rank
Birds won't fly in heavy rain or strong wind, so this is the show most likely to be pulled
Vultures and eagles come in low over the crowd — stay wide, they are faster than you expect

routeCard.note: Included in the day ticket. Sit on the grassed slope for the cleanest sky behind the birds.

see: Eagles, vultures and owls in flight
planCard.todo: Last outdoor stop of the day — after this the sun stops mattering. Stay wide and let them fly into frame rather than chasing them.
film: Birds coming in low over the crowd, wide
Falconer with bird on the glove, close
One line to camera: that's the outdoor half done

lunch.name: Lunch — thirty minutes
lunch.angle: Halfway, and the hard part is already filmed
lunch.story: You are at the halfway point with all three set-pieces in the bag and the sun-dependent half of the day behind you. Eat fast, swap the battery, check you actually got the jousting audio. Everything from here is indoors, which means the sky can do what it likes.
facts: All three outdoor shows are done by 1:05 PM — the weather can't hurt the film after this
Everything remaining is inside: State Rooms, the Mill, Lord Leycester, the chapel
Castle food is expensive; the town is better and cheaper but a 10-minute walk each way
Swap the battery now, not when you're halfway up the church tower

state-rooms.name: Great Hall & State Rooms
state-rooms.angle: Act four — fortress becomes a stately home
state-rooms.story: A castle only stays a castle while somebody still needs to defend it. The Greville family took Warwick in 1604 and spent the next three hundred and seventy years turning a fortress into a house. The Great Hall and State Rooms are that process made visible — and largely a rebuild, because a serious fire gutted part of the range in 1871. This is where the story stops being about war and starts being about money, taste, and keeping up appearances.
facts: The Grevilles held Warwick from 1604 until 1978 — 374 years
A major fire in 1871 gutted part of the range; much of what you walk through is the rebuild
In 1978 the family sold the castle to Madame Tussauds — fortress, to stately home, to attraction
Capability Brown landscaped the grounds from 1749, one of his earliest independent commissions

routeCard.note: Low light indoors — handheld, brace against door frames rather than pushing the ISO.

planCard.todo: This is the turn in the story — say out loud that the castle stops being a weapon here and starts being a house.

mill-engine.name: Mill & Engine House
mill-engine.angle: The Victorian machine under a medieval fortress
mill-engine.story: Down by the river under Caesar's Tower is the Mill and Engine House, where the Victorians put in generators to give the castle electric light. It is the least famous thing on site and one of the most interesting: a medieval fortress wired up by engineers in overalls. It also hands you the best low angle on Caesar's Tower anywhere in the grounds, and the broken bridge arches you filmed this morning are right outside — same subject, opposite bank, six hours apart. That cuts together well.
facts: The mill site is medieval; the machinery is Victorian — hydroelectric power for the castle
The castle had electric light before most of the town did
The ruined medieval bridge arches sit just outside — the same ones from your opening shot
Best low-angle view of Caesar's Tower on the entire site

routeCard.note: Steps down and back up. Last castle stop — leave by 2:40 for the walk into town.

see: The medieval bridge arches from the far bank
planCard.todo: Get the low angle on Caesar's Tower and the reverse of your opening shot. Then leave the castle — 10-minute walk to Lord Leycester.
film: Low angle up Caesar's Tower

lord-leycester.name: The Lord Leycester
lord-leycester.angle: The other man in this story
lord-leycester.story: Ten minutes from the castle gate is a row of crooked timber buildings that started life as 14th-century guildhalls. In 1571 Robert Dudley, Earl of Leicester and Elizabeth I's favourite, turned them into a home for wounded and retired soldiers. It still is one — the Brethren have lived here for 455 years. They also survived the Great Fire of Warwick in 1694, which flattened most of the town centre, and that is exactly why they look nothing like the Georgian brick all around them.
facts: Founded 1571 by Robert Dudley, Earl of Leicester, Elizabeth I's favourite
Still houses ex-servicemen — the Brethren — 455 years on
The buildings are 14th-century guildhalls; Dudley repurposed them, he didn't build them
Survived the Great Fire of 1694 — which is why the rest of the centre is Queen Anne brick
Show your Warwick Castle ticket at the desk: 25% off, £9 instead of £12, and a year's free return

routeCard.sub: High Street · open till 5, last admission 4
routeCard.note: Buy at the door, NOT online — the 25% castle discount only works at their ticket office.

planCard.todo: Show the castle ticket for 25% off. Set up the Dudley link here — you're about to stand at his tomb, and the audience needs to know who he is first.
film: Courtyard wide — the timber framing is the shot
Piece-to-camera introducing Dudley: 1571, still a soldiers' home

beauchamp-chapel.name: St Mary's — The Beauchamp Chapel
beauchamp-chapel.angle: Act five — the ending. They're all in here.
beauchamp-chapel.story: This is where the film ends. The Beauchamp Chapel was built between 1443 and 1464 to hold Richard Beauchamp, 13th Earl of Warwick, and it took twenty-one years because nobody was prepared to do it cheaply. His effigy is gilt bronze, hands raised. Robert Dudley is buried here too — the same man whose almshouse you walked out of twenty minutes ago — and so is his little son, who died at three. So you spend an entire day inside the rooms these men built and fought over, and then you stand at their graves. Say that on camera, and stop talking.
facts: Built 1443–1464 — twenty-one years — for Richard Beauchamp, 13th Earl, who died in 1439
His effigy is gilt bronze, one of the finest medieval tombs in Europe
Robert Dudley, Earl of Leicester, is buried here — the founder of the Lord Leycester
So is Dudley's son, who died aged three, known as the 'Noble Imp'
Church entry is free by donation; the chapel and chancel are £5; the tower is another £5 and 163 steps
The tower was rebuilt after the Great Fire of 1694

routeCard.note: Open from 10:30 on Saturdays and closes at 5, so 3:30 is comfortable. Chapel and chancel are £5 on the door.

planCard.todo: Pay the £5 for the chapel — this is the ending, not an optional extra. Film the sign-off in here, then put the camera down. Hard stop.
film: Slow push in on the gilt-bronze effigy — your closing shot
Dudley's tomb, with the line back to the Lord Leycester
Sign-off piece-to-camera in the chapel or on the church steps

signOff.where: In the Beauchamp Chapel, or on the church steps — 3:55 PM
facts: One sentence: whose tomb this is and why he mattered
The link back: 'that's the castle we started at this morning'
The ask: like, subscribe — and where should the next one go?

talkTipbox: You're telling this one yourself, so give each stop ONE idea, not five. Say the date, say what happened, say why it matters — then stop. 20–40 seconds a clip. Fluffing a line is fine: pause, breathe, go again. The edit will never show it.
goldenRules: Book the castle ticket online — cheaper, and it's your Rainy Day Promise insurance
Keep the physical castle ticket: it's the key to 25% off Lord Leycester
Confirm show times on the board at the gate — they move
Outdoor stops before 1:05 PM while the sun's out; everything after is indoors
Do each piece-to-camera BEFORE the show starts, not over the top of it
Handheld only — no tripod or gimbal without permission
Hard stop at 4 PM. Lord Leycester's last admission is 4; St Mary's shuts at 5.
outro: One castle, 958 years, and you finish standing at their tombs. That's a film, not a tour.
